about: The scripted AI lesson for p3-pressure (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p3-particle-model.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about the pressure a gas makes: what causes it, and how heating or squashing a gas changes it.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. How do the particles in a gas move?

options.text: They slide past each other, touching

steps.right: Yes: gas particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.

wrong.other: Not quite: fast, in random directions.
wrong.vibrate: Not quite: vibrating about fixed places is a solid. Gas particles move fast in random directions.
wrong.slide: Not quite: sliding past each other while touching is a liquid. Gas particles move fast in random directions.

idk.hint: A gas spreads out to fill any container. Are its particles held in place?

steps.answerWhy: Gas particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.

steps.question: Second: a gas gets hotter. Which is true of its particles?
steps.right: Yes: the hotter a gas, the faster its particles move on average.

wrong.other: Not quite: they move faster on average.
wrong.slower: Not quite: that is the wrong way round. A hotter gas has faster particles on average.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles do not change size. In a hotter gas they move faster on average.

idk.hint: Temperature is linked to the kinetic energy of the particles. What does more kinetic energy mean?

steps.answerWhy: A hotter gas has particles with more kinetic energy, so they move faster on average.

steps.text: Now this lesson. The particles of a gas move at a range of speeds, some fast and some slow, in random directions. They keep hitting each other and the walls of their container.
When a particle hits a wall it bounces off. Each hit like this is called a collision, and it pushes on the wall with a tiny force.
Billions of collisions every second add up to a steady push on every part of the wall. The push acts at right angles to the wall.
Pressure is the force on each square metre of a surface: pressure = force ÷ area. Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa): 1 Pa is a force of 1 newton on each square metre.
The push of all these collisions on each square metre of the walls is called the gas pressure.

steps.question: What causes the pressure of a gas in a sealed box?

options.text: Particles colliding with the walls of the box

steps.right: Yes: each collision with a wall pushes on it, and together they make the pressure.

wrong.other: Not quite: particles colliding with the walls of the box.
wrong.each: Not quite: particles do hit each other, but only hits on the walls push on the box. Collisions with the walls cause the pressure.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles never change size. Their collisions with the walls cause the pressure.

idk.hint: The pressure is a push on the box. What touches the box?

steps.answerWhy: Gas pressure is caused by the particles colliding with the walls of the container.

steps.text: Still air in a closed room presses on the walls too. Even when the air as a whole is not moving, its particles never stop.

steps.question: A balloon is blown up and tied. Why does it stay round?

options.text: Air particles inside collide with the rubber, pushing outwards everywhere
The rubber pulls itself into a ball
Air fills the gaps between the rubber particles

steps.right: Yes: collisions push outwards on every part of the rubber, at right angles to it, so the balloon stays round.

wrong.other: Not quite: air particles inside collide with the rubber, pushing outwards everywhere.
wrong.rubber: Not quite: the stretched rubber pulls inwards. It stays round because air particles collide with it from inside, pushing outwards everywhere.
wrong.gaps: Not quite: the air is inside the balloon. Its particles collide with the rubber, pushing outwards everywhere.

idk.hint: What is the air inside doing to the rubber, all over its inside surface?

steps.answerWhy: Air particles inside collide with every part of the rubber, pushing outwards at right angles to it.

steps.prompt: In one line: what causes gas pressure?
points: particles colliding with the walls of the container
each collision pushes on the wall with a force
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: gas particles collide with the walls of their container, and each collision pushes on the wall with a force.

keyPoints.heading: Temperature and pressure at constant volume

steps.text: Keep a gas in a sealed, rigid container, so its volume cannot change: the gas is at constant volume.
The temperature of a gas goes up with the average kinetic energy of its particles: the hotter the gas, the faster its particles move on average.

steps.question: A sealed metal can of gas is heated. Predict: which is true of the pressure inside?

options.text: It stays the same, as the volume is fixed

steps.right: Yes: the pressure rises. Next, why.

wrong.other: Not quite: it rises. Next, why.
wrong.fall: Not quite: it rises. Next, why.
wrong.same: Not quite: the volume is fixed, but the pressure still rises. Next, why.

idk.hint: Hotter means faster particles. Would faster particles push on the walls more or less?

steps.answerWhy: Heating a gas at constant volume makes its pressure rise.

steps.text: Heating makes the particles move faster. They hit the walls more often each second, and each collision pushes harder, so the pressure rises.
Cooling does the opposite: slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard, so the pressure falls.

steps.question: Which explanation of why a hot tyre has a higher pressure would score full marks?

options.text: Faster particles hit the tyre walls more often each second, and harder
The particles collide with each other more
The particles get bigger and push on the tyre

steps.right: Yes: faster particles, more collisions with the walls each second, a bigger force in each one, so a bigger force on each square metre.

wrong.other: Not quite: faster particles hit the tyre walls more often each second, and harder.
wrong.each: Not quite: only collisions with the walls push on the tyre. Faster particles hit the walls more often each second, and harder.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles never get bigger. They move faster, so they hit the walls more often each second, and harder.

idk.hint: Pressure comes from collisions with the walls. Which option is about the walls?

steps.answerWhy: Faster particles hit the walls more often each second and harder, so the force on each square metre is bigger.

steps.question: A student writes: "there are more collisions". What must they add to score the mark?
steps.right: Yes: examiners want collisions with the walls, and per second (or more often).

wrong.other: Not quite: "with the walls, each second".
wrong.between: Not quite: collisions between particles do not cause pressure. Add "with the walls, each second".
wrong.vibrate: Not quite: gas particles move about freely; they do not vibrate in place. Add "with the walls, each second".

idk.hint: The mark needs where the collisions happen and how often. Which option says both?

steps.answerWhy: The answer needs "more collisions with the walls each second".

steps.prompt: In one line: why does heating a sealed gas raise its pressure?
points: they hit the walls more often each second
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often each second and harder, so the pressure rises.

keyPoints.heading: Pressure and volume at constant temperature

steps.text: Now keep the temperature fixed and change the volume instead, like pushing in the plunger of a sealed syringe.

steps.question: A sealed syringe of air is squashed to half its volume, at the same temperature. Predict: which is true of the pressure?

wrong.other: Not quite: it doubles. Next, why.
wrong.halve: Not quite: it doubles. Next, why.
wrong.same: Not quite: it doubles. Next, why.

idk.hint: The same particles now have half the space. Will they hit the walls more often or less often?

steps.answerWhy: Squashing a gas into half the volume at the same temperature doubles its pressure.

steps.text: In half the space, the same particles hit each part of the wall twice as often each second. Their speed has not changed, because the temperature has not.
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume stays the same: p × V = constant. p is the pressure in pascals (Pa) and V is the volume in cubic metres (m³).
Two quantities linked like this are called inversely proportional: when one doubles, the other halves.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A gas has a pressure of 200 kPa and a volume of 3 m³. It is squashed to 1.5 m³ at the same temperature. What is its new pressure?
steps: Find p × V at the start: 200 × 3 = 600.
p × V stays the same, so afterwards p × 1.5 = 600.
Divide both sides by 1.5: p = 600 ÷ 1.5 = 400 kPa.

steps.text: You can keep pressures in kPa and volumes in cm³, as long as the before and after values use the same units.

steps.question: Your turn. A gas at 100 kPa has a volume of 6 m³. It is squashed to 2 m³ at the same temperature. What is its new pressure, in kPa?

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 kPa. 100 × 6 = 600, so p × 2 = 600 and p = 300 kPa.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 300 kPa. It is pressure × volume that stays the same, not pressure ÷ volume: 100 × 6 = 600, so p = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 kPa.
wrong.times: Not quite: 300 kPa. 100 × 6 = 600; then divide by the new volume: p = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 kPa.

idk.hint: First find p × V at the start: 100 × 6. Then divide it by the new volume, 2.

steps.question: Air in a syringe is at 100 000 Pa with a volume of 30 cm³. At the same temperature it is pushed in until its pressure is 150 000 Pa. What is its new volume, in cm³?

wrong.wrongway: Not quite: 20 cm³. Higher pressure means a smaller volume: 100 000 × 30 = 3 000 000, so V = 3 000 000 ÷ 150 000 = 20 cm³.

idk.hint: Find p × V at the start: 100 000 × 30. Then divide by the new pressure, 150 000.

steps.question: A gas expands into a bigger volume at constant temperature. Which is true?

options.text: Its particles hit the walls less often

steps.right: Yes: the particles are further apart, so they hit the walls less often, and the pressure falls. Their speed stays the same.

wrong.other: Not quite: its particles hit the walls less often.
wrong.slower: Not quite: the temperature is fixed, so their speed stays the same. They are further apart, so they hit the walls less often.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles never change size. They spread further apart, so they hit the walls less often.

idk.hint: The temperature is fixed, so the speed is too. With more space, how often does each particle reach a wall?

steps.answerWhy: At constant temperature the speed stays the same; with more space the particles hit the walls less often, so the pressure falls.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does squashing a gas at constant temperature raise its pressure?
points: the particles have less space (closer together)
they hit the walls more often each second
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a smaller volume the particles hit the walls more often each second, so the pressure rises.

steps.text: In an earlier lesson you met work done: when a force moves something, it transfers energy, and that energy is the work done.
Push a piston into a gas, as in a bicycle pump, and your force moves the gas: you are doing work on the gas.
The energy goes into the internal energy of the gas: the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles. With more internal energy, the gas warms up.
A bicycle pump gets warm when you pump up a tyre quickly for this reason: each push does work on the air inside.

steps.question: Why does the air in a bicycle pump get warmer as you push the handle in again and again?

options.text: Work done on the air raises its internal energy
The air particles rub together and make heat

steps.right: Yes: each push transfers energy to the air, so its particles move faster and its temperature rises.

wrong.other: Not quite: work done on the air raises its internal energy.
wrong.rub: Not quite: your push transfers energy to the air. That work done raises its internal energy, so its temperature rises.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles never change size. Work done on the air raises its internal energy, so the particles move faster.

idk.hint: Your force moves the gas. What does a force transfer when it moves something?

steps.answerWhy: Work done on the air transfers energy to it, raising its internal energy and so its temperature.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does a bicycle pump get warm?
points: work is done on the air (the gas)
its internal energy rises, so its temperature rises
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: pushing the handle does work on the air, raising its internal energy, so its temperature rises.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: what causes gas pressure?
steps.right: Yes: particles colliding with the walls.

wrong.other: Not quite: particles colliding with the walls.

steps.answerWhy: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a sealed jar of gas is cooled. Which is true of its pressure?
steps.right: Yes: slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard.

wrong.other: Not quite: it falls. Slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard.

steps.answerWhy: Cooling slows the particles, so they hit the walls less often and less hard: the pressure falls.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a gas at 200 kPa and 4 m³ is squashed to 2 m³ at constant temperature. What is its new pressure, in kPa?
Quiz, question 4 of 6: a gas at 50 kPa and 10 cm³ expands to 25 cm³ at the same temperature. What is its new pressure, in kPa?

wrong.other: Not quite: 20 kPa. 50 × 10 = 500, so p = 500 ÷ 25 = 20 kPa.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: a gas is squashed at constant temperature. Which is true of its particles' average speed?
steps.right: Yes: the temperature is fixed, so the speed is too.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays the same, because the temperature is fixed.

steps.answerWhy: At constant temperature the average speed of the particles stays the same.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: why does pumping a tyre quickly warm the air in the pump?

options.text: Work is done on the air
Cold air escapes from the pump

steps.right: Yes: work done on the air raises its internal energy and its temperature.

wrong.other: Not quite: work is done on the air, raising its internal energy.

steps.answerWhy: Work done on the air raises its internal energy, so its temperature rises.
